text: The last step of any real software project isn't writing more code — it's reviewing what exists against the requirements, finding the gaps honestly, and deciding what's actually done versus what's deferred with a reason. This lesson closes the capstone and the course the same way a real team would close a sprint.

This lesson covers running a full code review of quantumlib against lesson twenty-one's requirements line by line, distinguishing a genuine gap from a deliberately deferred, documented scope decision, a final checklist spanning every chapter of this course, and writing an honest known-limitations section.

Going back through the requirements: construction separated from execution is met, backend is always a parameter, never imported directly. Parametrized construction tests and the statevector check are met for Bell and GHZ, but not yet extended to the QAOA module. The statistical test with documented confidence is met. Resource-estimation functions are met and regression-locked for both Grover and QAOA. And experiment records for reported results aren't implemented yet — no experiments have been run and reported, only library code built. This table is the actual deliverable of a code review, not a vague 'looks good.'

Two of those 'not met' items are different in kind. The QAOA statevector check is a genuine, acknowledged gap — the right fix is scoped future work, not a decision that it's unnecessary. Experiment records aren't a gap at all — Chapter 4's reproducibility machinery exists specifically for reported results, and this capstone hasn't reported any experimental results yet, only built library code and run its test suite. Treating every unmet line identically, as either all fine or all broken, produces a worse review than naming each gap's actual nature.

A known-limitations section states explicitly: the QAOA module lacks a statevector-based construction check, tracked as an open issue; no experiments have yet been run and reported using this library, even though the reproducibility workflow is documented; and real-hardware validation hasn't been performed for any module. A documented limitation like this is categorically more trustworthy than a silent gap a user discovers themselves later.

Every practice in this course — tiered testing, backend abstraction, pinned dependencies, experiment records, resource estimation before submission, honest documentation of what's actually been validated — applies identically to real quantum research code and production quantum software, at any scale. The capstone was small, three algorithms, specifically so the practices would be the thing you walk away having actually done, not just read about. That closes Advanced Quantum Software Engineering.
